To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there is evidence of long-range atmospheric transport of several novel brominated flame-retardants, short-chain chlorinated alkanes and dechlorane, and that some current-use pesticides are also transported to the Arctic, but the question of whether or not they are bioaccumulated remains unanswered.

1) the Arctic environment is exposed to novel flame retardants that have been used to replace the banned PBDEs, and some of these compounds are transported to the Arctic; 2) some current-use pesticides have been detected in the Arctic, and their concentrations are increasing; and 3) the Arctic food web is exposed to novel brominated compounds, and some of them have been found to biomagnify.

(1) the Arctic environment is exposed to a wide range of contaminants, some of which have never been monitored systematically, (2) there are several indications that some of these contaminants may be transported to the Arctic and (3) for some of the compounds that are transported to the Arctic, there is evidence of bioaccumulative potential.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of new contaminants in the Arctic and with their fate in the Arctic environment.
the detection of new contaminants in the Arctic, but the data available for most of them are too sparse to allow for any firm conclusions.
the detection of new contaminants in the Arctic and the documentation of their long-range transport and/or bioaccumulation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a need for more systematic monitoring of new and current use chemicals, including those compounds that are not commonly monitored.

the evidence of long-range and bioaccumulation is not yet sufficiently documented for the majority of these compounds, but the available evidence indicates that some of the new contaminants are transported to the Arctic, and some are also bioaccumulating.
the evidence of long-range atmospheric transport and biomagnification of novel brominated compounds is still weak.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is increasing evidence of long-range atmospheric transport and bioaccumulative properties for a number of novel flame retardants and current-use pesticides.

the evidence is not yet sufficient to conclude that the novel compounds have reached the Arctic and that they are bioaccumulated and biomagnified, but the evidence of long-range and atmospheric transport and the potential for bioaccumulation and biomagnification is increasing for some compounds.
there is a clear need for systematic chemical monitoring of the Arctic environment for a number of new contaminants.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Arctic environment is still a sink for a number of new and current use contaminants and that the potential for bioaccumulation is high.
there are several novel contaminants that have been detected in the Arctic, and for some of them, long-range transport and/or bioaccumulation has also been observed.
the number of new and current use contaminants that have been detected in the Arctic environment has increased significantly over the last 15-20 years.
